topics.title: PoK Protests
bullets: At least 7–11 people were killed, with some reports placing the toll even higher, as protests raged ahead of scheduled elections over economic hardships and political representation In PoK.
Authorities responded by banning the protest group, filing sedition charges, and offering rewards for the arrest of its leaders.
A recent Pakistan Supreme Court verdict upholding 12 reserved seats for Kashmiri refugees living in Pakistan has become the immediate flashpoint for the current unrest. History and Creation of PoK –
When British India was partitioned in August 1947, the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir had not yet decided whether to join India or Pakistan.
In October 1947, tribal raiders backed by Pakistan invaded the state, prompting Maharaja Hari Singh to sign the Instrument of Accession with India on 26 October 1947.
Indian troops were subsequently airlifted into Srinagar, legally acceding the entire princely state of Jammu and Kashmir to the Union of India.
Following Maharaja Hari Singh's accession to India, the first India- Pakistan war broke out as Pakistani forces and tribal militias attacked the Kashmir Valley.
The conflict lasted through 1948, with Indian forces successfully defending the territory and pushing back the invading forces.
In January 1949, a ceasefire brokered by the United Nations brought the active hostilities to an end.
On 27 July 1949, India and Pakistan signed the Karachi Agreement, establishing a formal ceasefire line supervised by UN military observers.
This ceasefire line temporarily bifurcated Jammu and Kashmir, with India getting control of about 65 per cent of the state and Pakistan holding the remaining 35 per cent.
This line eventually became known as the Line of Control (LoC) after the 1972 Shimla Agreement.
The Pakistan-controlled territories cover about 78,000 sq km and came under Pakistani control following the 1 January 1949 ceasefire.
The territory is occupied by Pakistan, which has divided it into two separate administrative units: Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) and Gilgit-Baltistan.
India considers the entire territory of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, including PoK, Gilgit-Baltistan and the Shaksgam Valley, as an integral and inalienable part of India.
Gilgit-Baltistan was formed in 1970 as a single administrative unit under the name "Northern Areas" by amalgamating the Gilgit Agency, the Baltistan District, and the states of Hunza and Nagar.
In 1963, Pakistan ceded the Shaksgam Valley of Gilgit-Baltistan to China in a border agreement, further violating India's territorial integrity. Source - ThePrint Political Structure of PoK –
PoK operates under the Azad Jammu and Kashmir Interim Constitution Act, 1974, which was passed by the Legislative Assembly of AJK and approved by the Government of Pakistan.
The Interim Constitution provides for an apparently transitory autonomous parliamentary framework, including a President, Prime Minister, Legislative Assembly and judiciary.
The preamble of the 1974 Constitution states that the legal status of the territories is yet to be determined and that the Constitution is merely a temporary solution pending UN mediation.
Under the 1974 Interim Constitution, the executive authority of AJK is exercised in the name of the President by the Government, consisting of the Prime Minister and Ministers.
Pakistan has long presented the territory's President, Prime Minister, Assembly and flag as symbols of autonomy, but real power remains with Islamabad and Rawalpindi.
The Interim Constitution grants the Legislative Assembly no authority over defence, security, currency, external affairs, and trade — all key subjects are controlled by Pakistan.
Under Article 32 of the Interim Constitution, the Legislative Assembly cannot make any laws relating to defence and security of the territory, currency, external affairs and trade.
Historically, much of Pakistan's influence over PoK flowed through the Kashmir Council, a powerful institution headed by Pakistan's Prime Minister.
Although constitutional "reforms" in the 1970s altered parts of that framework, real authority over key matters continues to rest with Pakistan's federal government and military establishment.
Politicians, judges and constitutional office-bearers in PoK are required to take a mandatory oath affirming support for Kashmir's accession to Pakistan.
This requirement bars alternative political views from entering the mainstream and forces representatives to align with Islamabad's agenda.
Unlike Pakistan's provinces, where no such test exists, this ideological litmus test ensures complete loyalty to Pakistan's position on Kashmir.
Under the PoK Constitution, 12 seats in the 53-member Legislative Assembly are reserved for Kashmiri refugees settled in different parts of Pakistan, including Punjab and Sindh.
The election of these members happens outside PoK geographically as well as operationally, as the local Election Commission does not conduct the polling.
Locals say these seats are effectively used by the federal government to get their people into the PoK Assembly, bypassing local representation.
Apart from the 12 refugee seats, the PoK Assembly also reserves five seats for women, one for Ulamas (religious scholars), one for Kashmiris living overseas, and one for "technocrats."
In a House of 53, PoK voters directly elect only 33 people, the remaining 20 seats are filled through refugee and reserved- seat mechanisms.
The locals argue that since they do not elect these 20 representatives, they should not have to pay for them using PoK's funds, which fuels the current protests. Other Disputed Areas – Hyderabad –

Hyderabad was the largest and richest princely state in India, spanning nearly 83,000 square miles with a population of over 14 million, comprising present-day Telangana and parts of Karnataka and Maharashtra.
Its ruler, Mir Osman Ali Khan, the seventh Nizam, was then the richest man in the world, commanding a fortune that made him an important figure in the Muslim world.
Strategically located in the Deccan heartland, Hyderabad bisected the Indian territory like a "dagger poised at the nation's core"; Patel famously described it as "a cancer in the belly of India".
The Nizam declared his intention to keep Hyderabad as an independent sovereign state, neither joining India nor Pakistan, and refused to sign the Instrument of Accession.
In November 1947, India and Hyderabad signed a Standstill Agreement, which maintained the status quo for one year, during which India would not exercise authority over the state.
The Nizam, emboldened by Pakistan's Jinnah and hoping for British recognition, also made overtures to Portugal for a corridor to the sea through Goa, heightening Delhi's suspicions.
Taking advantage of the Standstill Agreement and India's preoccupation with the Kashmir war, the Nizam's administration increased the strength of its irregular paramilitary force called the Razakars.

Led by the fiery orator Qasim Razvi and Maj Gen SA El Edroos, the Razakars enforced a vision of Islamic primacy through terror, committing looting, abductions, and massacres on Hindu villages, displacing thousands.
The Razakars' belligerence along state borders through cross-border raids, coupled with their overtures to Pakistan, made military intervention inevitable.
On 13 September 1948, India launched Operation Polo, deploying about 35,000 troops from Solapur in the west and Vijayawada (Bezwada) in the east.
The Hyderabad state forces numbered less than 25,000, with only a fraction being well-trained; the Razakars were ill-trained volunteers who proved to be more of a nuisance than a military opposition.

By 17 September 1948, just five days after the operation began, the Nizam's forces surrendered, and Hyderabad formally signed the Instrument of Accession, becoming part of the Indian Union. Junagadh –
Junagadh was a small princely state in the Kathiawar region of present-day Gujarat, with an area of 3,336 square miles, a coastline on the Arabian Sea, and a population of approximately 545,000.
Crucially, Junagadh did not share any land border with Pakistan; it was entirely surrounded by Indian territory and had a majority Hindu population of about 80%.
Despite this, its ruler, Nawab Muhammad Mahabat Khanji III, a Muslim of Afghan descent, decided on 15 August 1947 to accede to Pakistan, arguing that Junagadh joined Pakistan "by sea".

The Nawab's Diwan (chief minister) was Shah Nawaz Bhutto, the father of future Pakistani Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who reportedly saw Junagadh's accession as a bargaining chip for the larger prize of Kashmir.
Jinnah waited for a month to formally accept the Instrument of Accession, likely to gauge international reaction and use Junagadh as leverage in the Kashmir dispute.
India refused to accept Junagadh's accession to Pakistan, and imposed a naval blockade, cutting off Junagadh's access to the sea.
Samaldas Gandhi, the nephew of Mahatma Gandhi, formed a provisional government demanding accession to India.
On 25 October 1947, as the situation turned against him, Nawab Mahabat Khan fled Junagadh in the dead of night.
Following the Nawab's flight, India took administrative control of Junagadh in November 1947 and, in a move to respect the principle of self-determination, agreed to hold a plebiscite.
In February 1948, the plebiscite was conducted in which the people of Junagadh voted overwhelmingly to join India, with only 99 votes cast in favour of Pakistan out of over 200,000 voters.
Junagadh was subsequently integrated into the Indian Union and later became part of the Saurashtra state, now within the present-day state of Gujarat. Beginning of Protests –
Residents of PoK first mobilised in May 2023 against rising electricity bills, flour smuggling and shortages of subsidised wheat.

The protests were fuelled by complaints that despite hosting major hydropower projects such as the 1,450 MW Mangla Dam and the 969 MW Neelum-Jhelum project, locals continued to pay exorbitant electricity tariffs.
By September 2023, the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) was formed by traders, professionals and activists.
In May 2024, protests spearheaded by JAAC escalated dramatically over soaring electricity bills and food inflation despite the region's abundant hydropower.
The protests included a long march toward Muzaffarabad, the capital of Pakistan-administered Kashmir, which attracted widespread attention.
Pakistan's then Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif responded by announcing a package of concessions, including subsidies on wheat and electricity and a reduction in flour prices.
By August 2024, the JAAC broadened its demands beyond economic grievances, calling for systemic political and governance reforms.
The group began demanding the abolition of the 12 reserved refugee seats, arguing that these seats gave Islamabad and Rawalpindi an additional lever of influence over electoral outcomes.
The JAAC also demanded that PoK's elected representatives be given genuine decision-making authority rather than serving as mere extensions of Pakistan's federal government. Supreme Court Ruling –
On 7 June 2026, the Pakistan-administered Kashmir Supreme Court ruled that the 12 legislative seats reserved for Kashmiri refugees living in Pakistan are constitutionally protected.
The court held that the refugee seats could not be abolished through executive action and that any change would require a constitutional amendment by the Legislative Assembly.
The court also directed that the 27 July 2026 legislative elections proceed as scheduled and should not be delayed due to the dispute over reserved seats.
Following the Supreme Court verdict, clashes erupted between police and JAAC protesters in Rawalakot, the capital of Poonch district in PoK.
According to official reports, at least 7 civilians were killed during Sunday's clash, while other sources reported 11 people including four security personnel died in the violence.
The clashes resulted in a complete shutdown across PoK, with markets closed and normal life paralysed.
The Pakistani establishment responded by banning the Joint Awami Action Committee as an unlawful organisation.
The AJK government announced a PKR 10 million reward for information leading to the arrest of four JAAC leaders, and ordered sedition proceedings against two JAAC figures.
The government also reinstated 177 FIRs against JAAC members, intensifying the legal crackdown on protest organisers.
On 5 June 2026, India's Ministry of External Affairs formally lodged a "strong protest" with Pakistan over the planned elections to the Gilgit-Baltistan Assembly.
Gilgit-Baltistan has never been made a full province of Pakistan because doing so would weaken Pakistan's claim on the entire Jammu and Kashmir.

The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) passes through this region, which India has consistently opposed as a violation of its territorial sovereignty.
